prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the biologically active peptide that made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: B024 is the one candidate on which all six opening ballots agree, but I do not rest the case on that. It meets the test I would apply to any candidate: a specific discovery that changed a field. Proglucagon processing, the identity of the active truncated GLP-1 peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and satiety actions, and the idea that this physiology could be made into a drug form a coherent causal chain. That chain has been confirmed independently over decades, by mechanistic work and by large randomized outcome trials. The impact is already large and visible in clinical practice (diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal outcomes). Holst (physiology of the active peptide), Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active form) and Drucker (peptide biology and the therapeutic concept) cover the discovery side of that chain without padding. Maturity is not a concern, and a further delay is hard to justify.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is contested and involves people outside the credited list, notably Habener, so a three-person limit may reward a disputed version of the history. Excluding Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues are the drugs patients actually receive, can also be criticised: it means the prize honours the physiology rather than the medicine. A related worry is that unanimous opening support may mask unresolved disagreement about what the citation should reward, basic discovery or drug development, and the committee should not let consensus hide that question.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked B024 first and B011 (CAR-T with June, Sadelain and Rosenberg) second, and also ranked imatinib (B047) and mTOR above several other candidates. He noted that Knudsen's work is important but industrial.
responses.response: I agree that Knudsen's contribution is real, and I do not think the 'industrial' label should count against it. The discovery-level credit is still stronger for Holst, Mojsov and Drucker, since the peptide identity and physiology are what made the drugs possible. I disagree mildly on B047. Its downstream clinical proof is decisive, but the upstream BCR-ABL biology is not credited on this list, which leaves a real gap in the story that B024 does not have to the same degree.

responses.point: Sandberg placed B011 second and B042 (HPV virus-like particle vaccines) third, favouring Rosenberg as a third CAR-T name and stressing population-level prevention effects.
responses.response: I put B011 clearly behind B024, and I would keep Rosenberg out. His adoptive-cell-transfer and TIL work is a distinct contribution that is better treated as a precursor than as part of the CAR discovery, and including him blurs the citation. On B042 I accept that its public-health impact is strong and measurable, but the supplied names leave out an important deceased co-inventor and the priority claims among VLP groups are contested, so I would not elevate it above CAR-T or the UPR.

responses.point: El Manira ranked optogenetics (B045) second, as a transformative method for circuit analysis, and placed B024 first with a three-person basic-science trio.
responses.response: I agree with his three-person basic-science trio for B024. On B045 I share his respect for the method, but I rank it lower. Six credited names against a three-person limit leave Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck outside any workable configuration, and the medical impact is still early. For a tool prize in this category I would want that attribution question resolved before supporting it, so I would not use it as a partner part.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (B034) second, as a model of bench-to-bedside immunology, while flagging her own field and noting that Mojsov's credit needs careful review.
responses.response: I agree that Mojsov's credit needs review, and I take that caution seriously. I read Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form as a real and necessary step, but the committee should not assume it is uncontested. On B034, the case is strong and fully mature, but it would be a late recognition of a clinical translation, and the antibody-engineering and TNF-discovery contributions sit outside the supplied names. I put it behind CAR-T and the UPR for that reason.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, ranked B011 with only June and Sadelain and B020 (UPR) third, treating Walter and Mori as a natural pair.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person form of B011 and with seeing Walter and Mori as the natural pair for B020. The difference is how the UPR credit is bounded: Ron's work on PERK and the integrated stress response is not on the credited list, so I would prefer to keep B020 as an alternative rather than a co-part with B024, because pairing parts makes the three-person limit force a worse GLP-1 trio.

uncertainties: Whether Holst, Mojsov and Drucker is a fair trio given contested peptide-identification priority involving people outside the list.
Whether the committee wants a citation that honours physiology and discovery, or one that also reaches drug development, in which case Knudsen would need to replace someone.
Whether a second part (CAR-T or the UPR) is worth the cost to the GLP-1 trio under the three-person limit.
I have not independently verified individual priority claims beyond the supplied credit lists.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B024 or the alternatives. My nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans and my dopamine-neuron research do not overlap with these candidates. I have co-authored with Per Svenningsson and, once, with Abdel El Manira; these are general collaborations, not a connection to any candidate on this shortlist.
